summary: Changes how DNSSEC cryptographic algorithm identifiers are allocated in IANA registries, from requiring a standards-track document to requiring only an RFC. It does not change which algorithms are recommended or required.

plainLanguage.summary: This is a change in registry paperwork. It makes it easier to get a number for a new DNSSEC algorithm, without changing which algorithms are advised.

subtitle: Loosens the requirement for new DNSSEC cryptographic algorithms to be documented in any RFC, not just standards-track ones.

tldr.problem: DNSSEC algorithm identifiers were restricted to algorithms defined in standards-track RFCs, making it hard to register algorithms with unclear intellectual property or insufficient maturity.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 6014 changes the allocation requirement to accept any published RFC, lowering the standards bar to get an algorithm registered.
tldr.outcome: RFC 6014 updates RFCs 4033, 4034, and 4035. Implementers still use only the algorithms required by RFC 4034; the change only affects registry enrollment, not protocol recommendations.

today: RFC 6014 updates RFC 4033, 4034, and 4035 to reflect the new allocation policy. It remains in force and is referenced in DNSSEC implementations and documentation.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
DNSSEC (DNS Security Extensions) uses cryptographic algorithms to sign and verify DNS records. Each algorithm has a numeric identifier in the IANA registry, so equipment can recognize which algorithm signed a record. Historically, RFC 2535 required that only algorithms defined in standards-track RFCs could receive an identifier.

This restriction meant that algorithms with unclear intellectual property rights, or those not deemed mature enough for standards track, had to use private values 253 or 254 instead, which required repeating an unregistered private name with each use.
sections.plainLanguage: Like a driver's license, algorithms need an official ID number to be recognized everywhere. The old rule said: only if you are completely standard. The new rule is friendlier.

sections.title: The Allocation Requirement Change
sections.content:
RFC 6014 changes the allocation policy from "IETF Standards Action" (standards track) to "RFC Required". Any published RFC can now sponsor an algorithm's registration, whether or not it is on the standards track. The document lists two reasons: some useful algorithms have intellectual property concerns or insufficient evaluation to make the standards track, and the registry has about 250 entries with infrequent additions, so it could take many decades to fill.

Alongside this change, IANA marked entries 123 through 251 as "Reserved" to slow the registry's filling and trigger future re-evaluation when most unreserved entries are taken. The registry now notes the standards status (standards track, best current practice, informational) of each RFC listed.
sections.plainLanguage: Before: your algorithm had to jump every hoop. Now: you just need to publish a proper document. Half the unused numbers are marked "reserved" to warn when we are running low.

sections.title: Implementation Expectations
sections.content:
The change does not alter which algorithms DNSSEC implementations must or should support. RFC 4034 defines mandatory-to-implement algorithms and recommends others; those lists stay the same. Implementations are not expected to support every algorithm in the registry. An algorithm on the registry does not mean every implementation must include it. The document notes that an algorithm not being on the standards track does not necessarily mean it is weaker; other factors like intellectual property concerns can keep strong algorithms off the standards track.

The order of algorithms in the registry does not signify cryptographic strength or preference. Implementations choose which algorithms to support based on their own needs and RFC 4034's requirements, not based on registry status.
sections.plainLanguage: Just because an algorithm is on the official list does not mean every program has to use it. The program builds its own rule about what it needs, separate from what is registered.

sections.title: Security of the Registry Change
sections.content:
By allowing non-standards-track algorithms, the registry may now include algorithms that are less thoroughly evaluated than those on the standards track. However, the document notes that standards-track status does not guarantee strength, and non-standards-track status does not necessarily indicate weakness. DNSSEC implementations retain control over which algorithms to trust; the RFC places the decision in their hands.

Developers who want to test experimental algorithms still have private-use values 253 and 254 available. This change does not affect those private values.
sections.plainLanguage: Some algorithms on the list might be newer and less tested. But you get to pick which ones your program trusts, so you are in charge of safety.

sections.title: Registry Management Considerations
sections.content:
RFC 6014 discusses why the IETF initially considered reserved slots for "experimental" or "documentation only" values, and why these were rejected. Experimental values in IETF history have a tendency to become permanent: once deployed, vendors resist changing them to an officially assigned value. Documentation-only values would not serve the purpose, since all values need to be associated with an actual algorithm.

When approximately 120 of the available 250 registry entries are assigned, the IETF is expected to re-evaluate the allocation policy, potentially tightening restrictions again or defining a new mechanism to extend the registry.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC explains why they did not make special numbers just for testing or examples: testing codes never stay temporary, people just keep using them. Real rules come later once half the numbers are taken.
